data.title: Unchanging peripheral vision desensitizes
data.contentMarkdown:
# Unchanging peripheral vision desensitizes

When the same stack of papers are on my desk for a month, I stop noticing them. [[z4geAr5cERWdJPrdhU5gy3N:::Peripheral vision]] only directs attention when {it changes somewhat consistently}. When {it stays the same}, it can actually desensitize the observer.

contextBlocks: My physical workspace is full of subtle cues. The books I read or bought most recently are lying out. Papers I’ve accumulated are lying in stacks on my desk, very roughly arranged by their relationship to each other. I notice a broken door every time I walk by it. These cues together give me a kind of “peripheral vision”: when I’m doing one thing, it’s easy for me to fluidly notice other nearby things. So long as the peripheral vision is reasonably dynamic, anyway—[[zYLNg1BLCBM9jECoNnHvysL:::Unchanging peripheral vision desensitizes]].

backlinkedNotes.linkingNoteTitle: When might desensitization be a useful design goal?
contextBlocks: Or, contrariwise, when might [[zYLNg1BLCBM9jECoNnHvysL:::Unchanging peripheral vision desensitizes]] be a danger?
